Notes & Conventions:
1. This page is deliberately technology-agnostic — no product or cloud-service name appears anywhere on it. Layers name roles, not products; see page 4 (Layered Solution Architecture, SAD §4 / §8) for the concrete technology mapping of every role shown here.
2. Cross-cutting concerns X1–X13 are drawn once in the right-hand column but apply to every layer above and below them — they are not a separate deployment tier.
3. M1–M16 are logical functional modules, not deployment units; several may be co-located or independently deployed depending on the target environment. Each module group owns its store in the data layer; the analytical store is fed by change-data capture, never queried on the request path.
4. The same logical architecture is realisable on cloud or on-premise infrastructure because every service ships as a container image and reaches infrastructure only through adapters (SAD §4, Deployment Options); Terraform versions each environment but does not by itself make a managed service portable. The Mobile App is a Phase 1 channel consuming the same Service Interfaces & API Facade unchanged.
5. Events leave a module through the transactional outbox relay; external providers call back in through the inbound callbacks (payment webhooks, delivery reports, email replies), and staff sign-in is federated with the enterprise identity provider.
6. The Policy Administration System and the finance / general ledger run in YCompany's data centre and are reached over a private link (navy dash-dot border), not the internet. The Partner System Interface and Partner Systems are Phase 2; the industry fraud database is checked at first notice of loss.

Notes & Conventions:
1. All external traffic is HTTPS / TLS 1.2+. Every API request carries an OAuth2 JWT (15-min access / 7-day refresh) issued by the Auth Service; each service checks the signature itself with the Auth Service's signing keys, cached locally. The ALB accepts traffic only from CloudFront, so WAF cannot be bypassed.
2. Every portal and the app upload straight to the S3 incoming prefix with a pre-signed POST, issued only after the Document Service has checked with the Claims Service that the user may add to that claim. The policy fixes the key incoming/{claimId}/{documentId}, the content types, a size range and the SHA-256 checksum. GuardDuty scans each object; a clean file moves to claims/{claimId}/…, its metadata row is written and DocumentUploaded is published, and the Claims Service attaches it to the claim.
3. A service writes the events listed in its box (⇢; ⇠ marks a consumer v2.0 added) to an outbox table in the same transaction; the relay publishes them to EventBridge, whose rules feed one SQS queue per consumer (each with a dead-letter queue) and start or advance the Step Functions workflow. A line from a service straight down to a database is SQL / TLS through RDS Proxy. The Notification Service reads contact details from the User / RBAC Service.
4. Layer 6 is cross-cutting; dashed flows are representative (KMS and AWS Backup → every database, audit trail → Audit DB → S3 Object Lock, Okta → Auth Service). Tasks with side effects check the Route 53 ARC routing control first, so only the active Region acts.
5. Solid arrows = request / data flow; dashed arrows = cross-cutting / association / Phase 2. External systems on the right carry their page 1 tags; event names follow the SAD §4 event catalogue.
6. v2.0: the Surveyor is assigned on AppointmentBooked or VehicleLocationSet; the Booking Service opens, extends and ends the rental on VehicleReceived, DeliveryDateChanged and VehicleDelivered; workflow ⑥ (Total Loss & Theft) runs on the /claims, /payments and Stripe hops, whose labels name it. D7 (ISO ClaimSearch, from the Fraud Detection Service) and E4 (General Ledger, from the Payment Service) are reached through the services' adaptors; E3 and E4 sit in YCompany's data centre behind a private link (navy dash-dot). Their lines are left out for legibility.

Why no managed API Gateway? Classic API-Gateway capabilities are already delivered by existing components (verified against the SAD):
Routing / dispatch → ALB (Multi-AZ, path routes /auth /users /admin /claims /assignments /documents /locations /bookings /repairs /payments incl. /payments/webhooks /messages /reports)   |   AuthN / AuthZ → Auth Service (OAuth2/JWT) + RBAC + Okta SSO, ALB OIDC offload
Rate limiting / throttling → AWS WAF + Shield Advanced (edge rate-based rules)   |   Caching → CloudFront (edge) + ElastiCache Redis (data, <100 ms)
Canary / blue-green → CodePipeline + CodeDeploy, ALB weighted target groups   |   Circuit breaker / retries → service-level breakers + exponential backoff
Distributed tracing → CloudWatch + X-Ray   |   Request validation → in-service (FastAPI + Pydantic)
A managed API Gateway would only add per-API-key usage plans / metering — not required in Phase 1, since partners use the Partner Portal; it is reconsidered for the Phase 2 partner API alone.

Notes & Conventions:
1. Route 53 (G1) is the network entry point — DNS resolution for every internet-facing request (SAD §4 Layer 2) — and the Region switch: CloudFront's origin hostname is a G1 failover record whose health checks follow the G4 routing controls (Note 15).
2. Every AWS component on this page and the CI/CD page uses real AWS Architecture Icons and proper AWS group containers (VPC/AZ/Subnet/Security-Group) — a departure from pages 1-4's plain colour-block convention, scoped to these two infrastructure pages only.
3. Phase 1 = two AWS Regions, each Multi-AZ (3 zones): us-east-1 (N. Virginia) is primary and serves all traffic; us-east-2 (Ohio) is a warm standby at minimum capacity. Multi-Region active-active remains out of scope (§10).
4. This page is the deployment-topology companion to page 4 — page 4 names every AWS service per logical layer; this page places the same services on a physical VPC/AZ/subnet network map.
5. V1–V10 are tagged once in us-east-1 and V1′–V10′ once in us-east-2, to avoid clutter; the other zones repeat the pattern untagged. RDS and ElastiCache Multi-AZ are a standard 2-AZ pair; us-east-1c's data subnet holds the third OpenSearch node for write quorum, the in-Region read replica (V8) and the Audit DB (V9).
6. The Data Subnet reuses the Private Subnet's group-container styling — AWS's icon set has no distinct "isolated subnet" container; isolation is conveyed by the label, not a different icon.
7. Where two connectors cross, the crossing is drawn as an arc jump; no two connectors share a parallel route.
8. The Auth Service is grouped under Layer 2 in SAD §4 for its logical capability, but physically runs as an ECS Fargate task in the private/app subnet alongside every other microservice.
9. Every component sits behind a Security Group; one is drawn illustratively around the us-east-1a Fargate icon rather than repeated on every instance.
10. AWS SNS and SES appear twice by design: N4 is the internal service (SMS, mobile push and SES delivery reports); D3/D4/D5 represent the last-mile hops out to the carrier, the mail server and the Apple and Google push services.
11. CI/CD (CodePipeline/CodeBuild/CodeDeploy/ECR, SAD §4 Layer 6/§8) has its own dedicated page (tab 6) rather than being drawn here — it's a deployment-time concern, not a runtime network path.
12. E3 (Policy Administration System) and E4 (General Ledger) are YCompany's own systems in its data centre, carried through from page 1. They are reached privately through the Transit Gateways (V11, V11′) and AWS Direct Connect (H1–H3), not through NAT Gateway egress (Note 25).
13. On-diagram captions are short names only; full descriptions, zone-specific variants and protocol detail are in the registry table above, indexed by the same G/V/N/D/E tags used on the diagram.
14. External SaaS is a right-side column adjacent to us-east-1c and sourced from that zone's NAT Gateway (V2) for short, direct routing — egress is identical from any zone's NAT Gateway. After failover, us-east-2's NAT Gateways (V2′) egress to the same providers (not drawn). SNS delivers mobile push to D5 itself. D7 ISO ClaimSearch is in this column; E3 has moved to the YCompany data centre (Note 25).
15. Failover (warm standby): on a us-east-1 outage the on-call runs the pre-approved runbook — promote the V4′ and V9′ replicas, promote N7′, point V7′ at V4′, pre-scale V3′, then flip the G4 routing controls (us-east-2 On, us-east-1 Off) so Route 53 answers with V1′. CloudWatch alarms page the on-call but never move traffic, and a recovered us-east-1 cannot take traffic back while its control is Off. Failback is the same runbook in reverse, after re-seeding us-east-1.
16. Replication and targets: RDS cross-Region read replicas (V4 → V4′ for each of the four instance groups, V9 → V9′), OpenSearch cross-cluster replication over inter-Region VPC peering (V6 → V6′), S3 Cross-Region Replication (N1 → N1′), Secrets Manager replica secrets (N7 → N7′), AWS Backup copies (N15 → N15′) and Redshift cross-Region snapshot copies (V10 → V10′). ElastiCache is not replicated and starts cold. EventBridge with its archive, SQS, SNS, Lambda, Step Functions and Scheduler (N2′–N6′) run in both Regions (Terraform); the Scheduler's jobs stay idle until the Region is active, and messages queued in us-east-1 are not replicated. Region failure: RTO < 30 min; RPO < 5 min for the database and < 15 min for S3 objects. AZ failure: RTO < 15 min, RPO < 5 min.
17. Held ready in us-east-2: SES production access, SNS SMS and mobile-push registration, partner and Stripe allow-lists for the V2′ addresses, V11′ associated with the Direct Connect gateway (H3), ACM certificates for V1′ and raised Fargate and Step Functions quotas.
18. Zone names (us-east-1a …) map to different physical zones in each AWS account; Terraform pins the zone IDs (use1-az…), so the names here are illustrative.
19. V1 and V1′ are drawn as one band per Region because an ALB is a single regional resource with a node in each zone's public subnet; the arrows from each band are its target group reaching the Fargate tasks in every zone.
20. Uploads: browsers and the app upload documents straight to S3 (N1) with pre-signed POSTs over TLS — the one internet path that does not pass G2/G3 — and GuardDuty Malware Protection (N13) scans each object before the Document Service accepts it. CloudFront serves the portals' static files from S3 through origin access control.
21. The ALB accepts traffic only from CloudFront (the CloudFront managed prefix list in its security group, plus a secret origin header), so WAF cannot be bypassed; Stripe's webhooks reach the Payment Service through G1–G3 like any other request.
22. Data: every service connects through RDS Proxy (V7) to its own database on V4's four instance groups (claims core, identity, high-volume records, money & fraud); the in-Region read replica (V8) takes the read-heavy work; the Audit DB (V9) is a separate instance written through an insert-only role; Redshift (V10) sits in the data subnets and is fed by zero-ETL integrations from the claims-core and money-and-fraud groups.
23. Tasks with a side effect (assignment, notification, payment, the outbox relay and the scheduled jobs) read the G4 routing-control state before acting, so only the active Region acts (dashed edge from V3).
24. Accounts: this page shows the production account. AWS Organizations keeps development, staging, production and a security and log-archive account apart; CloudTrail (N12) is an organization trail into the log-archive account, and Security Hub (N14) collects findings in the security account.
25. Hybrid connectivity: two AWS Direct Connect connections at diverse locations (H1) and a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup (H2) connect YCompany's data centre to a Direct Connect gateway (H3) associated with the Transit Gateway in each Region (V11, V11′). Private subnets route YCompany's address ranges to the Transit Gateway (dash-dot edge from V3), and traffic stays TLS-encrypted end to end. If E3 is confirmed to be hosted in AWS or as SaaS, PrivateLink replaces this path (SAD §4, Hybrid connectivity to YCompany).
26. G2 runs AWS Shield Advanced (response team, DDoS cost protection, health-based detection). A WAF rule admits the Internal Portal's hostname only from YCompany's corporate address ranges, and Okta starts a staff session only on a managed device. N19 Amazon Textract serves the document indexing Lambda (N5).

Notes & Conventions:
1. Reading order: Source (P1) → CodePipeline (P2) orchestrates five sequential stages via a shared S3 artifact bucket (P3) — Stage 1 Build & Scan (P4 → P5, scans Q4/Q5), Stage 2 Infrastructure (P6, Checkov + Terraform, manual approval gate), Stage 3 Pre-production (P17 → P14 → P15, mobile P19), Stage 4 Release approval (P16), Stage 5 Production (P7, blue/green, canaries P18).
2. Cost framing: CodePipeline charges a small flat fee per active pipeline with no idle-time charge; CodeBuild bills only actual build-minutes — no idle build server to provision, patch or scale. Materially cheaper than a self-managed Jenkins controller running around the clock, and avoids a second CI/CD tool alongside AWS's own managed equivalents.
3. Blue/Green mechanism: Blue = current/live (P10), Green = new candidate (P11); CodeDeploy (P7) shifts ALB weighted-target-group traffic (P8) — the mechanism behind SAD §7's "blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases."
4. Rollback: a CloudWatch (R1) alarm on ECS/ALB health or a failed Synthetics canary (P18) during the traffic shift triggers automated traffic-back-to-Blue and Green deregistration — ties to §7's Resilience/Reliability row.
5. CodeBuild appears three times (P4, P6, P15) — distinct projects (build and scan, Terraform, staging gates), one managed service; mirrors the Cloud/Deployment page's own SNS/SES dual-appearance note.
6. CloudWatch (R1) and Secrets Manager/KMS/IAM (Q1-Q3) also appear on the Cloud/Deployment page (N7-N10) — same services, two different lifecycle moments (steady-state runtime there, deployment-time here), not a duplicate.
7. This page is a companion to the Cloud/Deployment page — it does not redraw the VPC/AZ/subnet topology. The ECS Service/task-set icons here stand in for the same Multi-AZ Fargate runtime (V3 there); the ALB (P8) is the same regional ALB (V1 there), not a second load balancer; us-east-2's V1′/V3′ receive the same release through P13.
8. Q3 (IAM) is shown with no drawn edge, consistent with the Cloud/Deployment page's N9 — its role relationship applies uniformly to every pipeline stage.
9. Source Repository (P1) is GitHub, connected to CodePipeline through AWS CodeConnections; a push or merge to main starts the pipeline.
10. Multi-Region release: ECR replicates every image to us-east-2 (P12); Terraform (P6) applies the us-east-1 and us-east-2 stacks; after the us-east-1 deploy succeeds, a cross-Region CodeDeploy action (P13) runs the same blue/green into the us-east-2 warm-standby service, so both Regions run the same image. The pipeline and Terraform state live in us-east-1, so releases pause during a us-east-1 outage.
11. Security scans: Semgrep (static analysis), pip-audit and npm audit (dependencies) and gitleaks (secrets) run in P4 (Q5); Amazon Inspector scans every image pushed to ECR (Q4); Checkov scans the Terraform before plan (P6); OWASP ZAP scans the running staging stack (P15). A critical finding fails the stage.
12. Environments: the release is deployed to the development and staging accounts before production. Staging is production-like, so its gates (P15) — integration tests, a short k6 load test at the SAD §9.1 design point and the ZAP scan — run against the real topology.
13. Database changes: Alembic migrations run as a one-off ECS task (P17) before each environment's traffic shift, written expand-then-contract so the Blue and Green versions both work against the same schema.
14. Portals and mobile: the three portals' static bundles go to S3 with a CloudFront invalidation in each environment; the React Native app is built and signed in P4, distributed to TestFlight and Google Play internal testing from staging (P19), and released to the stores after its own approval.
15. Synthetics canaries (P18) run the first-notice-of-loss, status-check and approval journeys during the production traffic shift, alongside smoke tests, and every minute afterwards.

Notes & Conventions:
1. This page draws the on-premise profile of SAD §4, Deployment Options, as a physical topology. Product names are the profile's named options, not commitments; page 5 is the AWS profile of the same logical architecture (page 3).
2. Edge: a global server load balancer (O1) and a CDN and WAF service (O2) sit in front of both data centres. O2 forwards to the active data centre's ingress (O3); the runbook switches O1 to send traffic to O3′.
3. Zones mirror page 5's subnets: DMZ (public), application (private), data (isolated, no internet route) and management, separated by firewalls. Only the egress proxies (O4, O4′) reach the internet.
4. Auto-scaling is bounded by the hardware: the HPA scales pods, and the Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes only from a pre-provisioned pool (vSphere or OpenShift machine sets), so capacity for the 1,000 requests/s design point (SAD §9) is bought in advance.
5. Failover: the on-call runs the same pre-approved runbook as page 5 — promote the Patroni standby clusters and the audit standby, point PgBouncer at them, promote Vault, scale O5′, then switch O1. Camunda instances are per cluster, so each claim's instance is rebuilt in DC2 on its next action. Failback is the same in reverse.
6. E3 and E4 run on YCompany's internal network and are reached locally from both data centres (navy dash-dot); internet services go out only through the egress proxies, Stripe's webhooks come in through O1–O3 like any other request.
